extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (schemes and morphisms)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, basic properties, and key theorems about finiteness-type conditions on morphisms of schemes (finite, integral, finite type, finitely presented, quasi-finite) together with image-theory (Chevalley, elimination) and closed embeddings/closed subschemes. The material is aimed at learning/teaching how to recognize and use these properties in algebraic geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y that is finite (examples include the normalization map Spec k[t] → Spec k[x,y]/(y^2 − x^2 − x^3) given by (x,y) ↦ (t^2 − 1, t^3 − t)). Finite morphisms are affine (by definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key properties/exercises: (8.3.H) Composition of two finite morphisms is finite. (8.3.I) Finite morphisms to Spec A arise from certain graded constructions and are projective. Finite morphisms are affine and projective; they have finite fibers (8.3.J) and their images are closed (Exercise 8.3.L). Beware: having finite fibers alone does not imply finiteness (see Example 8.3.6 and Figure 19.1). Use Exercise 8.3.G to show finiteness to Spec k forces X to be a finite discrete union of points with finite residue fields (give explicit approach: integral domain finite k-algebra must be a field, primes are maximal, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is integral if for every affine open Spec B ⊂ Y with π^{-1}(Spec B) = Spec A, the induced ring map B → A is integral (i.e., A is integral over B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affine-local condition (Exercises 8.2.A, 8.2.B and the Affine Communication Lemma 5.3.2), closed under composition (Exercise 8.2.C). Finite morphisms are integral (Corollary 8.2.2) but the converse need not hold (example: Spec Q → Spec Q). Integral morphisms are closed maps (Exercise 8.3.L); however, unlike finite morphisms, integral morphisms need not have finite fibers (8.3.8). Fibers of integral morphisms have the property that no point is in the closure of another (see remark and Exercise 12.1.E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally of finite type / Finite type
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is locally of finite type if for every affine open Spec B ⊂ Y and every affine open Spec A ⊂ π^{-1}(Spec B) the induced map B → A expresses A as a finitely generated B-algebra. A morphism is of finite type if it is locally of finite type and quasicompact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent formulations via affine covers (Proposition 5.3.3(b)). Typical example: the structure morphism P^n_A → Spec A is of finite type (covered by n+1 affines). Common nomenclature: 'P = locally P + quasicompact' (Remark 8.3.10). Basic closure properties: open embeddings are locally of finite type and quasicompact open embeddings are of finite type; composition of morphisms locally of finite type is locally of finite type (8.3.P). Use these definitions to check finite-type hypotheses in exercises and theorems (e.g., Chevalley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi-finite morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is quasi-finite if it is of finite type and for all q ∈ Y the fiber π^{-1}(q) is a finite set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The point of the definition is the 'finite fiber' part; finite morphisms are quasi-finite (combine 8.3.J and 8.3.O(a)). There exist quasi-finite morphisms that are not finite (Example 8.3.6). Quasi-finite morphisms to Spec k are finite (Exercise 8.4.D). Zariski’s Main Theorem (exercise reference) explains how quasi-finite morphisms arise as finite maps with a closed locus of points removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finitely presented / Locally finitely presented morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A B-algebra A is finitely presented if A ≅ B[x1,...,xn]/(f1,...,fr) (finite generators and finitely many relations). A B-scheme X is locally finitely presented over B if it has an affine cover with each Ai finitely presented over B; a morphism π : X → Y is (locally) finitely presented if this holds for every affine open Spec B ⊂ Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If B is Noetherian, finitely presented = finite type (Exercise/Remark). The property of finite presentation is affine-local (Lemma 8.3.15 and Exercise 8.3.R) and can be characterized as limit-preserving: π is locally finitely presented iff Hom_Y(lim S_λ, X) = colim Hom_Y(S_λ, X) for affine projective systems (8.3.18). A morphism is finitely presented (finite presentation) if it is locally finitely presented, quasicompact, and quasiseparated (8.3.19). Several exercises (8.3.R–8.3.W) give techniques to check and manipulate finite presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite = integral + finite type (criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism is finite if and only if it is integral and of finite type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is posed as Exercise 8.3.O: (a) show finite ⇒ finite type, (b) prove the equivalence finite ⇔ (integral + finite type). Use this to deduce finiteness in practice by verifying integrality and finite-type hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructible subsets (and their characterizations)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Noetherian topological space, a constructible subset is one belonging to the smallest family containing all open sets and closed under finite intersections and complements. Equivalently, constructible subsets are finite disjoint unions of locally closed subsets (Exercise 8.4.A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful characterizations: a constructible subset is closed iff it is stable under specialization; open iff stable under generization (8.4.C). The preimage of a constructible set under a continuous map of Noetherian spaces is constructible. These facts feed into Chevalley’s theorem and elimination arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevalley’s Theorem (image constructibility criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is a finite type morphism of Noetherian schemes, the image of any constructible set is constructible; in particular, im(π) is constructible (Theorem 8.4.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences and uses: gives a quick proof of the Nullstellensatz (8.4.3), implies surjectivity of maps of varieties can be checked on closed points (8.4.F), and is the geometric underpinning of elimination of quantifiers statements (8.4.8–8.4.J). Proof strategy outlined: reduce to affine cases, reduce to A^1_B and closed/locally-closed subsets, then analyze polynomial degrees and use finiteness of certain induced morphisms (8.4.4–8.4.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of quantifiers / Fundamental elimination results
rubrics_metrics.description: Given polynomials f_i and g_j with parameters w in an algebraically closed field k, the set of parameter values w for which there exists x solving f_i(...,x)=0 and g_j(...,x)≠0 is a Zariski-constructible subset of k^m (8.4.J). The Fundamental Theorem of Elimination Theory (8.4.10) states that the projection π : P^n_A → Spec A is closed (images of closed sets are closed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequences: classical elimination constructs (determinants, resultants) arise as equations on coefficients that characterize existence of nontrivial solutions. Proofs use graded ring/linear algebra arguments (8.4.5 and 8.4.11). No Noetherian hypothesis is needed for the projective (closedness) statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed embedding / Closed subscheme
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is a closed embedding (closed immersion) if it is affine and for every affine open Spec B ⊂ Y with π^{-1}(Spec B) ≅ Spec A the map B → A is surjective (i.e., A ≅ B/I for some ideal I). A closed subscheme of Y is a subscheme whose underlying map is a closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties and exercises: closed embeddings identify X topologically with a closed subset of Y but the scheme structure (infinitesimal data) matters (9.1.A). Closed embeddings are finite morphisms (9.1.B), compositions of closed embeddings are closed embeddings (9.1.C), and the property is affine-local on the target (9.1.D). Closed subschemes correspond bijectively to quasi-coherent sheaves of ideals on Y via the exact sequence 0 → I_{X/Y} → O_Y → π_* O_X → 0 (9.1.2); conversely every quasi-coherent ideal sheaf gives a closed subscheme (9.1.F). Use affine-local descriptions (Spec B → Spec B/I) to construct and recognize closed subschemes.
